## objective

Explain with measurements why `sam-tagger pileup` needs about 3 hours per
run on the ecsngsqc S34_1 data (analysis run `01a1ed14`). Decide whether
CPython-level code is the bottleneck. Rank possible speedups. The task is an
investigation: proposals only, no change to sam-tagger source.

## scope

1. Read-only inputs: the pipeline workspace `WS` (two BAMs, the reference
   FASTA, the original pileup Parquet files, the rule logs).
2. All new files go to `SCRATCH`
   (`/bioproj/t/20261125.agent.sam-tagger-pileup-perf`), with its own git
   repository and its own pixi workspace.
3. In this repo: this plan, the matching report, and `docs/misc/*`.
4. Not in scope: changes to `src/`, `pixi.toml`, `pyproject.toml`, `tests/`.

## planned steps

1. Preconditions: time, load, memory, repo head, tool versions.
2. Secondary and supplementary record counts of both BAMs.
3. Two full pileup runs, concurrent as in the original. Run A (`all`) is the
   clean baseline under `/usr/bin/time -v`. Run B (`ap_both`) runs under
   py-spy at 50 Hz. A detached sampler records CPU and RSS every 60 s.
4. Subsample profiling on a 1 % subset of the reads: py-spy (raw stacks with
   line numbers, and a flamegraph), cProfile, and floor measurements
   (`samtools view -c`, pysam iterate-only, pysam plus the per-record reads,
   the full pileup).
5. Prototype in SCRATCH: dense arrays per reference, one cached plan per
   (start, cs tag), numpy match runs, batches per key. Equality check against
   the original output, then a concurrent A/B on a subset that keeps the
   read depth (all reads of every 100th reference).
6. After the full runs: the timing table against the originals, the stage
   split, the profile shares of run B, the output comparison against the
   original Parquet files, and the full-size prototype check on both BAMs.
7. Report, audit entry, rolling docs, Lark note.

## what happened

1. The scheduled job fired at 19:17, 76 minutes late, on a machine with a
   load average of 13 to 26 on 12 logical CPUs (6 cores). CPU time and
   same-time comparisons replaced wall-clock as the measure.
2. Wrote this plan, created the scratch directory with its own git
   repository and pixi workspace, then started run A at 19:21 and run B at
   19:22. Both ran detached with `setsid nohup`. A sampler wrote CPU and RSS
   every 60 s. A background waiter and a durable one-shot cron collected the
   results. The cron moved with the delayed schedule (21:45, 23:20, 00:05,
   01:05) and was deleted after the report.
3. Counted secondary and supplementary records: 0 in both BAMs. The outputs
   of head 0.9.0 must therefore equal the 0.8.0 originals.
4. Profiled a 1 % subset of the reads (997,411 records) with py-spy,
   cProfile and floor measurements in the repo environment: 81.78 % of the
   samples inside `tally_from_record`, 10.01 % in the per-record pysam
   reads, 5.74 % in the output phase. Floors: pysam iteration 0.99 µs of CPU
   per record, all per-record reads 11.84 µs, full loop 171.1 µs.
5. Built a second subset that keeps the read depth (all reads of every 100th
   reference: 454 references, 1,014,154 records). The uniform subset is not
   representative for a design with a plan cache.
6. Wrote the prototype `dense_pileup.py`: dense arrays per reference, one
   cached plan per (start, cs tag), numpy match runs, batches per key. Four
   defects of the prototype were found and corrected before the first exact
   result: a startup-order error, an empty column placeholder in the output
   stage, the allele string in the numeric part of an indel row, and the
   reference base missing on insertion and deletion rows. It reproduces the
   original output exactly on three subsets. A concurrent A/B on 1,014,154
   records gives a CPU ratio of 5.0 and 4.3 for the per-read mode. Per-key
   batching adds a factor of 1.45.
7. Found that the quality filter ignores the leading soft clip (test with a
   crafted `3S27M` record). The task changes no source, so this is a finding
   only.
8. Run A ended at 23:01:04: 13,186 s wall, 12,540.5 s CPU, maximum RSS
   11,946 MB, output phase 29 s. Run B ended at 23:14:29: 13,931 s wall.
   Both outputs equal the originals row for row. The full-run profile holds
   88.15 % of 695,906 samples inside `tally_from_record`, 10.72 % in the
   per-record pysam reads, and 0.17 % in the output phase.
9. The full-size prototype check ran on both BAMs from 23:16: 30 m 46 s and
   31 m 04 s, output exactly equal, 1,783.7 s and 1,801.2 s of CPU, 7.7 GB
   maximum RSS through the Parquet write.
10. Wrote the report first as a draft in the scratch directory, then as
    `docs/plans/20261125-235011_pileup-perf-investigation.report.qmd`, and
    rendered it.

## risks

1. The job started at 19:17, not at 18:01. The machine carried a load
   average of 13 to 26 on 12 logical CPUs (6 cores). Wall-clock is inflated
   by CPU contention: 1.23 to 1.30 times the original runs. CPU time
   (user + sys) is the primary measure, and ratios come from runs at the
   same time.
2. Head 0.9.0 skips secondary records; the originals ran 0.8.0. Both BAMs
   hold 0 secondary records, and the outputs are equal, so the versions do
   not differ on this data.
3. A session restart during the long runs: the runs were detached, and a
   durable follow-up cron was in place. No restart happened.

## verification

1. The timing table in the report holds measured wall-clock, user CPU, sys
   CPU and max RSS for both full runs. The CPU time of run B is a sampler
   estimate, because GNU time measured py-spy and not the worker.
2. The profile shares come from the py-spy raw stacks of full run B (695,906
   samples) and of the 1 % subset (22,337 samples). cProfile gives the call
   counts.
3. Each proposal carries a measured basis: the concurrent A/B and the
   full-size runs for the dense-array design, the py-spy line shares and the
   floors for the per-record trims, the floors for the compiled-loop
   estimate.
4. The new Parquet files of the two full runs and of the two prototype runs
   are compared with the originals with `assert_frame_equal(check_exact=True)`.
   All four are equal.
